entities.summary:
The Battle of Cnidus was a pivotal naval engagement in the Corinthian War, fought between the Achaemenid Empire and the Spartan fleet in 394 BC. This decisive victory marked a significant shift in the balance of power in the ancient Mediterranean, as the Achaemenid Empire's naval supremacy was cemented. The battle's outcome had far-reaching consequences for the region, as the weakened Spartan fleet struggled to recover from the loss.

The Achaemenid fleet, led by Pharnabazus and Conon, successfully exploited the inexperience of the Spartan commander, Peisander. The Spartans had previously enjoyed a brief naval ascendancy, but the Battle of Cnidus brought an end to this period of dominance. The Achaemenid Empire's victory had a lasting impact on the region, shaping the course of naval warfare in the ancient world.

The legacy of the Battle of Cnidus can be seen in the subsequent rise of the Achaemenid Empire as a major naval power. This, in turn, contributed to the spread of Persian influence throughout the ancient world, leaving a lasting cultural footprint. The battle's impact also resonated in the Roman Republic, where it was studied and emulated by military strategists.

In the words of the ancient historian, Xenophon, 'The Battle of Cnidus was a turning point in the history of the ancient world, marking the beginning of the end of Spartan naval supremacy.'

The Battle of Cnidus was a defining moment in the history of the ancient world, marking a significant shift in the balance of power and shaping the course of naval warfare.
